newsitem.title: FRANCE: African force takes over from French in Bangui.
newsitem.headline: African force takes over from French in Bangui.

text.p: An inter-African peacekeeping unit has taken over from French troops in the divided Central African capital Bangui and officials in France said they hoped it would be a model for an African force Western powers want to create.

"The transfer of authority (from French to African troops) took place yesterday, February 12, and has been warmly greeted locally," a senior French defence ministry official told reporters in Paris on Thursday.

The new force is the Inter-African Mission to Monitor the Bangui Accords (MISAB) and its 450 men from six countries are to serve as a buffer between army mutineers and the presidential guard which are recruited from rival tribes.
French troops had handled the chore so far but they became identified by the rebels as being pro-government and had themselves become involved in the fighting in recent months.

"As of today, French troops are still in some MISAB areas because we can't pull everyone out right away," the official said. "But normal life is resuming in Bangui where schools and medical facilities have all re-opened."

MISAB was created in December as a result of accords drawn up between rival sides who have been at odds on ethnic grounds since several mutinies last year turned into a campaign to oust President Ange Felix Patasse.
The official said France hoped MISAB would be the model or core for an African rapid reaction force which both Paris and Washington have separately sought to create.
MISAB is composed of six small units from Chad, Gabon, Mali, Burkina Faso, Senegal and Togo which were equipped by France at its permanent base in Libreville, Gabon.

The force is commanded by Senegalese Colonel Talla Niang but Paris will continue to play a major role since its logistics are provided by a French army service unit sent specially to handle everything from its food to its transport.

"Our hope is that this will serve as basis for an inter-African peace force. Of course, every situation requires a different answer but it is obvious that what we are heading for is that Africans take over African affairs and this is what is happening," the French official said.

"France and other Western countries have been talking about an African peace force for three or four years now and it is obvious that here, the first time such a force has really been set up politically and militarily, we hope the consequences for the future will be drawn," he said.

French troops remain however based outside Bangui and in the provincial town of Bouar to guarantee against external attack and serve as a springboard for French military activity elsewhere on the continent.
The number of French troops in the country, which rose to over 2,000 late last year will soon return to its normal figure of 1,200 men near Bangui and 600 in Bouar, the official said.
They are backed by four Mirage fighter-bombers and five Transall C-160 transport aircraft.
